newsitem.title: UK: British part-time workers to get equal rights-TUC.
newsitem.headline: British part-time workers to get equal rights-TUC.

text.p: Britain's six million part-time workers are set to get a legal right to equal treatment with their full-time counterparts, the Trades Union Congress said on Friday.
The TUC said an agreement has been signed by European trade unions and employers, including Britain's top bosses organisation, the Confederation of British Industry.
The draft agreement has been agreed by the executive committee of the European TUC and UNICE, the European employers' group.

The TUC statement said the agreement would be formally signed at a Social Dialogue summit on Friday, in the presence of the Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and the President of the European Commission Jacques Santer."
It will then go to the European Commission's Social Affairs Council later this year and if accepted, will be adopted as a directive which will become law in Britain in two years' time.

"Part-time workers are a valuable part of the workforce," said John Monks, TUC General Secretary. "This groundbreaking agreement between Europe's trade unions and employers means that at long-last, part-time workers will be able to enjoy the flexibility of working part-time without fear of discrimination."

The TUC said British part-time workers have had equal statutory rights over unfair dismissal and redundancy since early 1995. But they do not yet have the same contractual rights -- covering such things as paid holidays and sick leave, company pensions, staff discounts and share options.
Eighty percent of Britain's part-timers are women. At present, they can only claim unfair treatment on the grounds of sex discrimination.
But Monks said that many of Britain's biggest companies already give part-time staff full equal rights. "They clearly find this helps their business not hinders it," he said.
